title: The Human Labial Superficial Musculoaponeurotic System (SMAS). Anatomy, Imaging, Biomechanics, Sensory Function, Aging and Clinical Implications
content: Background/Objectives: The superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) is a fundamental anatomical concept in facial surgery, but its existence and organization within the human lips remain incompletely understood. This review critically reassesses the anatomical evidence for a specialized labial fibromuscular connective tissue system and evaluates its relationship to the facial SMAS. Methods: Published anatomical, histological and imaging evidence was integrated with current knowledge of connective tissue biology and with original anatomical and magnetic resonance observations described in the manuscript. Particular attention was given to the relationships among the connective tissue framework, orbicularis oris, dermis, vermilion and oral mucosa, as well as to biomechanical, sensory, aging and clinical implications. Results: The available evidence consistently shows a highly organized fibromuscular framework that establishes structural continuity between the orbicularis oris and superficial soft tissues. Its architecture differs from the classical cheek SMAS and is better interpreted as a regional specialization adapted to the distinctive mechanical demands of the perioral region. Connective tissue septa also provide pathways for neurovascular structures and are closely related to sensory corpuscles. Apparent discrepancies among previous studies largely reflect differences in anatomical definition and terminology rather than incompatible morphological observations. Conclusions: Current anatomical, histological and imaging evidence supports a specialized fibromuscular connective tissue organization within the human lips. Whether it is termed a labial SMAS depends principally on the anatomical definition adopted. Recognition of this integrated framework provides a coherent basis for understanding lip morphology, biomechanics and sensory organization and has direct relevance to reconstructive, aesthetic and minimally invasive procedures.
